papers.title: Single-cell Morphological Mechanisms-of-Action Profiling using Nanowell Imaging Plates.
papers.abstract: Mechanism-of-action (MoA) analysis is used in drug discovery to prioritize compounds that act through desired pathways while eliminating compounds associated with nonspecific or undesirable activity. Image cytometry provides a promising route for MoA inference by capturing high-dimensional cellular phenotypes at single-cell resolution, but conventional workflows remain limited by unreliable cell segmentation and dependence on human-engineered feature extraction. Here, we present a deep learning-based image cytometry workflow that confines single cells in nanowells to obtain uniformly framed, r
papers.journal: SLAS discovery : advancing life sciences R & D
papers.summary: The authors present a deep learning-based image cytometry workflow that uses nanowells to confine single cells, enabling uniform imaging and more reliable morphological profiling for mechanism-of-action analysis in drug discovery. This approach aims to overcome limitations of conventional workflows such as unreliable cell segmentation and dependence on hand-engineered features.

papers.title: Surrogate Machine Learning Models for ADME Prediction: From Synthetic Labels to Experimental Data.
papers.abstract: Optimization of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) properties is central to small-molecule drug discovery, yet is often constrained by limited access to large and consistent experimental data sets. The performance and generalizability of machine learning (ML) models for ADME property prediction rely on the composition of the training data. Surrogate data sets comprise compounds annotated with synthetic ADME labels (predictions) generated by ML models trained on experimental data. This can offer a consistent data augmentation or sharing strategy without requiring access
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: This paper examines surrogate machine learning models for ADME prediction, where synthetic labels generated by models trained on experimental data are used to augment or share training data without exposing proprietary experimental sets. It evaluates how the composition of such surrogate data affects model performance and generalizability for ADME property prediction in small-molecule drug discovery.

papers.title: DrugMAP 3.0: an enriched molecular atlas featuring ADMET endpoints, pharmacogenomic perturbations, and bioactivity atlas of drugs.
papers.abstract: The paradigm of targeted therapeutics has shifted from static drug-target interactions to systemic absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) endpoints, dynamic transcriptomic perturbation signatures, and quantitative binding affinities, thereby amplifying the demand for multidimensional pharmacological atlases. In other words, it is necessary to bridge systemic safety profiles, cellular responses, and molecular interactions. However, such integrative data were inadequately covered by existing databases. In this study, DrugMAP was therefore substantially updated, whi
papers.summary: DrugMAP 3.0 is a substantially expanded database that integrates three previously fragmented dimensions of drug pharmacology: ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity) endpoints, transcriptomic perturbation signatures, and quantitative drug-target binding affinities. By consolidating systemic safety profiles, cellular responses, and molecular interactions into a single multidimensional atlas, it addresses a gap in existing drug databases that typically cover only one of these layers. The resource is intended to support drug repurposing, safety assessment, and mechanistic studies of drug action.

papers.title: AI-Driven Discovery of Nodakenin as a Novel Molecular Glue Targeting the TRIM28-NR4A1-LCN2 Axis to Induce Ferroptosis in Melanoma.
papers.abstract: Melanoma remains a malignancy requiring novel interventions. While triggering ferroptosis has emerged as a promising anti-tumor strategy, the targetable molecular vulnerabilities governing this process remain incompletely understood. Here, through artificial intelligence (AI)-driven virtual screening, we identified the coumarin derivative Nodakenin (NK) as a potent inhibitor of nuclear receptor subfamily 4 group A member 1 (NR4A1), an orphan nuclear receptor highly expressed in malignant melanoma cells. Transcriptomic, biochemical, and structural analyses revealed that NK triggers ferroptosis
papers.summary: Using AI-driven virtual screening, the authors identified the coumarin derivative Nodakenin as an inhibitor of the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A1, which is highly expressed in malignant melanoma cells. Biochemical and structural analyses indicate that Nodakenin acts as a molecular glue along the TRIM28-NR4A1-LCN2 axis, triggering ferroptosis in melanoma cells. This work nominates a new compound and a targetable pathway for melanoma therapy.

papers.title: Targeting protein degradation strategies in drug discovery: integrating PROTACs, ubiquitination biology, and AI-driven design.
papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy for eliminating disease-associated proteins, including targets that remain challenging to modulate using conventional occupancy-driven inhibitors. Among TPD approaches, proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) exploit the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) to induce selective and event-driven degradation of proteins of interest (POIs). Despite rapid advances in PROTAC development, successful translation depends on interconnected determinants, including target degradability, ubiquitin ligase (E3) recruitment,
papers.summary: This review examines targeted protein degradation (TPD) as a therapeutic strategy, focusing on PROTACs that hijack the ubiquitin-proteasome system to eliminate disease-causing proteins rather than merely inhibiting them. It discusses key determinants of successful PROTAC translation—target degradability, E3 ligase selection, and linker design—and highlights how AI-driven approaches are being integrated into the design pipeline. The paper frames TPD as a convergence of ubiquitination biology, medicinal chemistry, and computational design.

papers.title: Existing Drugs Targeting Genes of Hereditary Pain Syndromes as Candidates for Analgesic Repurposing: An AI-Facilitated Computational Knowledge Discovery Analysis.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Over the last few decades, hereditary syndromes with extreme pain phenotypes have guided the discovery of analgesic drugs. We hypothesized that genes of hereditary syndromes with altered pain perception, not necessarily the extreme phenotypes grouped as hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies, could also point to existing drugs with unrecognized analgesic properties via known interactions with syndrome-relevant gene products. Methods: Phenotypes with altered pain mentions were retrieved from the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database, and their genes w
papers.summary: This study used AI-assisted computational knowledge discovery to test whether genes underlying hereditary pain syndromes could point to existing drugs with unrecognized analgesic potential. By mining OMIM phenotypes with altered pain perception and mapping their genes to known drug-gene interactions, the authors identify candidate drugs for analgesic repurposing. The work suggests that hereditary pain genetics can guide drug discovery beyond the classic extreme-phenotype neuropathies.

papers.title: From Gene Lists to Druggable Hubs: An Integrative In Silico Framework for Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres.
papers.abstract: Between 10 and 15% of cancers maintain their telomeres without telomerase, through a recombination-based route known as alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT). It is most common in sarcomas and gliomas. The mechanism itself is increasingly well understood, but the view from population-scale data is not: which components are perturbed most consistently across tumors, how they organize into networks, what they cost the cell metabolically, whether their expression says anything about outcome, and which existing drugs might exploit them. Here we bring together four in silico studies that used
papers.summary: This paper integrates four in silico analyses to characterize alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) in cancers, moving from gene lists to network hubs and candidate drugs. It examines which ALT pathway components are consistently perturbed across tumors, how they organize into networks, their metabolic costs, prognostic value, and potential for drug repurposing. The framework aims to identify druggable hubs in ALT-dependent cancers such as sarcomas and gliomas.

papers.title: Phytochemical Profiling and Biological Activities of Moroccan Juniperus phoenicea L. Leaf Extracts: UHPLC-MS Analysis, Molecular Docking, and ADMET Predictions.
papers.abstract: Juniperus phoenicea L. is a medicinal plant native to the Mediterranean region, including Morocco, where it is traditionally used to treat various ailments. This study aimed to characterize the phytochemical profiles of aqueous, ethanolic, and hydroethanolic leaf extracts of Moroccan J. phoenicea and evaluate their antioxidant, antibacterial, and antifungal activities. Potential interactions between the extracts and conventional antimicrobial agents were also investigated, alongside molecular docking analyses of selected phytochemicals and in silico predictions of their pharmacokinetic and tox
papers.summary: This study characterizes the phytochemical composition of Juniperus phoenicea leaf extracts using UHPLC-MS and evaluates their antioxidant, antibacterial, and antifungal activities, including potential synergistic interactions with conventional antimicrobials. Molecular docking and ADMET predictions were used to explore the binding of selected phytochemicals to target proteins and assess their drug-likeness. The work provides a chemical and bioactivity profile of a traditional Moroccan medicinal plant, but the findings are largely descriptive and in silico.

papers.title: Multi-Target Anti-Inflammatory Mechanisms of Stachyurus praecox Leaf Extract Revealed by Metabolomics, Network Pharmacology, Molecular Docking, and Experimental Validation.
papers.abstract: Inflammation is a major pathological process underlying numerous chronic diseases, highlighting the need for anti-inflammatory inhibitors from nature. This study investigated the anti-inflammatory potential of S. praecox leaf extracts and elucidated molecular mechanisms through an integrated experimental and computational approach. As a result, the 75% methanol extract (75M) inhibited tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) production in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated RAW264.7. Untargeted metabolomic analysis led to the tentative identification of 96 metabolites, predomin
papers.summary: This study investigates the anti-inflammatory properties of Stachyurus praecox leaf extract using an integrated approach combining untargeted metabolomics, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and experimental validation. The 75% methanol extract inhibited TNF-α and IL-6 production in LPS-stimulated macrophages, and metabolomic profiling tentatively identified 96 metabolites. The multi-target mechanisms were explored computationally and validated experimentally, suggesting the extract's potential as a natural anti-inflammatory agent.

papers.title: Computational Hazard Prioritization of Aerosolized E-Cigarette Flavoring Additives Using Virtual Knockout, Molecular Dynamics, and Human Genetic Follow-Up.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Inhaled e-cigarette flavoring additives contact oral and respiratory epithelia, yet chemical-specific testing priorities and molecular hypotheses remain scarce. We combined chemical-screening and contextual gene-level branches to nominate priority flavorings and testable pathway hypotheses. Methods: Eight flavoring additives and carrier solvents were evaluated across 229 shared targets and 29 hubs via an 80-pair AutoDock Vina screen (exhaustiveness = 32), reference-inhibitor redocking, AlphaFold 3/Protein Data Bank checks, replicated 100 ns molecular dynamics, and ADMET/
papers.summary: This study combines computational docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and human genetic data to prioritize e-cigarette flavoring additives for toxicological testing. The authors screened eight flavoring additives and carrier solvents against 229 shared protein targets and 29 hub proteins, then used genetic follow-up to nominate priority chemicals and generate testable pathway hypotheses. The work provides a computational framework for hazard prioritization of inhaled flavorings rather than definitive toxicological conclusions.

papers.title: Computational Prediction of Elbasvir as a Theoretical Candidate for PFOS-Associated Gut and Skin Shared Pathologies.
papers.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) frequently co-occur along the gut-skin axis, yet the systemic triggers, particularly environmental endocrine-disrupting chemicals like perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate network toxicology and single-cell multi-omics to propose a computational framework for the shared molecular signatures of PFOS-driven AD and IBD comorbidity. Utilizing large-scale clinical transcriptomic cohorts and machine learning, we computationally predicted the transcription factor MYC as a potential core pathologic
papers.summary: This study uses network toxicology, machine learning, and single-cell multi-omics to identify shared molecular signatures linking PFOS exposure to the co-occurrence of atopic dermatitis and inflammatory bowel disease along the gut-skin axis. The authors computationally predict MYC as a core transcription factor and nominate the antiviral drug elbasvir as a theoretical therapeutic candidate. All findings are computational predictions without experimental validation.

papers.title: Molecularly Aged Protein States as Targets for Drug Design and Delivery in Neurodegenerative Diseases.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative drug discovery usually represents a protein target by its gene, canonical sequence, and one or a few structures. That representation can miss the molecular history accumulated by proteins that persist in the brain. Spontaneous chemistry, incomplete repair, altered turnover, proteolysis, phase transitions, and assembly remodeling generate states that may differ from the canonical target in exposure, function, and therapeutic accessibility. We call compositionally resolved species age-generated proteoforms and use molecularly aged protein states when the exact composition remai
papers.summary: This perspective argues that neurodegenerative drug discovery should move beyond representing protein targets by their gene, canonical sequence, and a few structures, because long-lived brain proteins accumulate chemical modifications, incomplete repair, altered turnover, proteolysis, and assembly changes over time. The authors propose 'age-generated proteoforms' and 'molecularly aged protein states' as concepts to capture this molecular history, which can alter target exposure, function, and therapeutic accessibility. They suggest these aged states could serve as new targets for drug design and delivery in neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: In Silico and In Vitro Studies on Selective MAO-B Inhibition and Predicted Microbiome Interactions of Novel Chalcone Derivatives: Relevance to the Gut-Brain Axis in Autism Spectrum Disorder.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) lacks pharmacological therapies for its core features. This study synthesized chalcone derivatives, determined their monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) and MAO-B inhibitory profiles, and generated computational hypotheses regarding MAO-B binding, gut-bacterial protein interactions, and drug-like properties. Methods: Sixteen chalcones (23-38; fifteen newly reported) were synthesized and characterized. MAO-A and MAO-B inhibition was measured using fluorometric concentration-response assays, with clorgyline and safinamide as references. Compounds 23,
papers.summary: This study synthesized sixteen novel chalcone derivatives and tested their ability to selectively inhibit MAO-B versus MAO-A, finding some compounds with promising selectivity. Computational docking and microbiome interaction predictions were used to hypothesize how these compounds might affect gut bacteria relevant to the gut-brain axis in autism spectrum disorder. The work is preliminary, combining in vitro enzyme assays with in silico predictions rather than demonstrating efficacy in disease models.

papers.title: Antioxidants from Onion (Allium cepa L.): Current Evidence, Redox Mechanisms, and an AI-Assisted Discovery Framework.
papers.abstract: Allium cepa L. (onion) is a globally important vegetable crop and functional food recognized for its rich diversity of antioxidant phytochemicals, including flavonoids, organosulfur compounds, phenolic acids, anthocyanins, saponins, and polysaccharides. Onion-derived phytochemicals have demonstrated antioxidant and redox-modulating activities in chemical, cellular, and animal studies. However, onion-specific applications of artificial intelligence and structure-based computational methods remain limited. This review therefore discriminates established experimental evidence from computational p
papers.summary: This review consolidates experimental evidence on antioxidant phytochemicals from onion (flavonoids, organosulfur compounds, phenolic acids, anthocyanins, saponins, and polysaccharides) and their redox-modulating mechanisms across chemical, cellular, and animal studies. It also proposes an AI-assisted, structure-based computational framework for discovering and prioritizing onion-derived antioxidant compounds, noting that such applications remain limited for this crop.

papers.title: Blood-Brain Barrier Permeability Prediction: Machine Learning, Graph Neural Networks, and Protonation-State Robustness.
papers.abstract: Blood-brain barrier permeability (BBBP) prediction is important for central nervous system (CNS) drug discovery, yet the relative performance of traditional molecular feature-based models and graph neural networks (GNNs), as well as the sensitivity of BBBP predictions to molecular protonation states, remains insufficiently characterized. Here, we curated the public OmniBBBP dataset through structural deduplication, label-conflict resolution, and removal of compounds overlapping with an external benchmark, yielding 8836 compounds for model development. Four traditional machine learning (ML) mod
papers.summary: The authors curated a cleaned public dataset (OmniBBBP) of 8,836 compounds for blood-brain barrier permeability prediction and compared traditional molecular-feature machine learning models against graph neural networks. They also examined how sensitive predictions are to molecular protonation states, an often-overlooked factor in CNS drug discovery.

papers.title: Machine Learning and Structure-Based Virtual Screening for Reliability-Aware G Protein-Coupled Receptor Ligand Prioritization.
papers.abstract: Background: Predictive performance is necessary but insufficient for G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) ligand prioritization, where heterogeneous bioactivity data, analog-series overlap, receptor-state dependence, and polypharmacology can weaken high-scoring predictions. Methods: We developed an auditable ligand- and structure-based workflow across five human GPCRs: DRD2, CB2, ADORA2A, OPRM1, and CCR5. ChEMBL Ki, IC50, and EC50 data were evaluated using scaffold-disjoint validation, external validation, Venn-Abers calibration, conformal prediction, applicability-domain analysis, explainability
papers.summary: The authors present an auditable virtual screening workflow combining ligand-based machine learning with structure-based docking across five human GPCRs (DRD2, CB2, ADORA2A, OPRM1, CCR5). They emphasize reliability-aware evaluation using scaffold-disjoint and external validation, Venn-Abers calibration, conformal prediction, applicability-domain analysis, and explainability to flag where high-scoring predictions may be unreliable. The work is a methodological contribution to GPCR ligand prioritization rather than a new biological finding.

papers.title: Toll-Like Receptors in Mycoplasma Infections: Immunopathogenesis, Cheminformatics, and Machine Learning-Based Insights into TLR-Targeted Therapeutics.
papers.abstract: Mycoplasma species are the minimal-genome pathogens that elicit complex host immune responses involving both protective and pathogenic inflammation. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are pivotal components of the immune system, recognizing pathogen-associated molecular patterns and damage-associated molecular patterns to initiate immune responses. TLRs recognize Mycoplasma-derived lipoproteins, glycolipids, and CpG-rich DNA motifs, initiating NF-κB and MAPK signaling cascades. While these pathways are indispensable for microbial clearance, their dysregulation contributes to chronic inflammation, auto
papers.summary: This review examines how Toll-like receptors recognize Mycoplasma components such as lipoproteins, glycolipids, and CpG-rich DNA, triggering NF-κB and MAPK signaling that can both clear infection and drive chronic inflammation. The authors combine immunopathogenesis discussion with cheminformatics and machine learning approaches to identify potential TLR-targeted therapeutics. It is a broad synthesis aimed at connecting basic immunology with computational drug-discovery strategies for Mycoplasma-related disease.

papers.title: Pharmaceutical Methotrexate Formulation Exposure Alters Growth and Biofilm of Pseudomonas aeruginosa with Exploratory Evidence for Folate-Pathway Involvement.
papers.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa remains challenging to control because of intrinsic antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated tolerance, highlighting the need to explore alternative therapeutic strategies. This study investigated the in vitro effects of a pharmaceutical methotrexate (MTX) formulation on P. aeruginosa PAO1, its interaction with gentamicin (GEN), and the potential relevance of selected folate-pathway proteins. Planktonic growth inhibition, growth kinetics, developing and preformed biofilm biomass, and biofilm-associated membrane integrity were evaluated. MTX-GEN interactions were e
papers.summary: This study shows that a pharmaceutical methotrexate formulation inhibits planktonic growth and affects both developing and preformed biofilms of Pseudomonas aeruginosa PAO1, with exploratory evidence implicating folate-pathway proteins. It also examines interactions with gentamicin, suggesting MTX may influence antibiotic efficacy. The work is preliminary and in vitro, but points to a potential repurposing avenue for biofilm-associated infections.

papers.title: Benchmarking Structural Models of α-Conotoxin-Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor Complexes: Apo-Conformer Selection, Interface Information, and Deep-Learning Co-Folding.
papers.abstract: Conopeptides are a proven drug source, but translation stalls at one step: predicting how a peptide engages a human receptor before a clinical program commits. We benchmarked modelling of α-conotoxin-nicotinic acetylcholine receptor complexes at two deposited structures, kept separate because their data-leakage status differs: a human α7-ImI cryo-EM complex, rated MEDIUM leakage risk, and a non-human Aplysia acetylcholine-binding protein-RgIA crystal that lies inside the Boltz-2 training window and is therefore a positive control, not a held-out test. Apo-conformer choice fixes attainable accu
papers.summary: This study benchmarks computational methods for predicting how α-conotoxin peptides bind to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, a key step in peptide drug development. The authors evaluate apo-conformer selection, interface information, and deep-learning co-folding approaches against two experimentally determined structures, carefully distinguishing a held-out human α7-ImI cryo-EM complex from a positive-control structure that falls within the Boltz-2 training window. The work highlights that the choice of apo receptor conformation strongly constrains achievable accuracy and that data-leakage status must be accounted for when benchmarking deep-learning co-folding models.

papers.title: Phytochemical Profiling and Preliminary In Vitro Assessment of Thai Traditional Medicine (Yahom Navakot) Extracts on HepG2 Cells, Integrated with ADMET and Molecular Docking Analyses of Selected Identified Compounds.
papers.abstract: Yahom Navakot (NV) is a traditional Thai polyherbal formulation with a long history of use in traditional medicine. However, its hepatoprotective potential and chemical characteristics remain incompletely characterized. This study investigated the biological activities and chemical profiles of aqueous and methanolic NV extracts using complementary in vitro and in silico approaches. The aqueous and methanolic extracts maintained human hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2) cell viability above 70% at 25-400 µg/mL. In a hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-induced oxidative stress model, the methanolic extract at
papers.summary: This study characterizes the chemical composition of Yahom Navakot, a traditional Thai polyherbal formulation, and tests its effects on HepG2 liver cells. Both aqueous and methanolic extracts were non-toxic at tested concentrations, and the methanolic extract showed protective effects against oxidative stress. The authors also used computational ADMET and molecular docking analyses to predict which identified compounds might contribute to these activities.

papers.title: In Silico Identification of a Potential Multi-Target Natural Compound Against Oral Cancer.
papers.abstract: Oral cancer remains a significant global health problem due to delayed diagnosis and limited treatment effectiveness. This study employed an integrated in silico approach to identify potential natural compounds from the family Ganodermataceae, targeting chemokine receptors CXCR3, CXCR4 and CXCR7. A library of 1300 mushroom-derived compounds was screened using a ligand-based pharmacophore. The best hits were subjected to molecular docking. The computational candidate, (+)-Applanatumol D, was further evaluated using ADMET, DFT, 200 ns MD simulations and MM-GBSA. Molecular docking predicted inter
papers.summary: The authors screened 1,300 mushroom-derived natural compounds against the chemokine receptors CXCR3, CXCR4, and CXCR7 using pharmacophore modeling and molecular docking, identifying (+)-Applanatumol D as a top multi-target candidate. They then assessed this compound with ADMET predictions, DFT calculations, 200 ns molecular dynamics simulations, and MM-GBSA binding free energy analysis. The work is entirely computational and proposes a natural compound for further experimental validation against oral cancer.

papers.title: Target-Specific Benchmarking of Potency Prediction on Activity-Cliff Compounds Across 33 Human Protein Targets Using Inhibition Constants.
papers.abstract: Activity cliffs are pairs of closely related compounds whose potencies differ far more than their structures suggest, and the compounds involved in them remain a leading cause of local failure in ligand-based potency prediction. The MoleculeACE benchmark established that models predict these compounds poorly and that the gap differs between datasets. What has been missing is a panel built on one activity endpoint, a per-target account of how large the gap is, and a measurement of how far it depends on the way the model is chosen. We curated inhibition constant (Ki) data for 33 human protein ta
papers.summary: This paper curates inhibition constant (Ki) data for 33 human protein targets to build a target-specific benchmark for evaluating potency prediction models on activity-cliff compounds—structurally similar molecules with unexpectedly large potency differences. It quantifies how poorly models predict these compounds per target and shows that the size of the prediction gap depends on how the model is selected. The work provides a standardized, single-endpoint panel for diagnosing where ligand-based potency prediction fails.

papers.title: Genome-Wide CRISPR Screening Identifies NAPRT as a Key Regulator of Human Adipogenesis.
papers.abstract: Adipocyte differentiation is central to adipose-tissue homeostasis, but its regulatory landscape remains incompletely defined in human cells. Here, we perform a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen in oleic acid-differentiated human SW872 preadipocytes to identify functional regulators of white adipogenesis. The screens nominate hundreds of adipogenesis-regulating genes, and integration with human genetic evidence prioritizes nicotinate phosphoribosyltransferase (NAPRT) as a prominent player. NAPRT loss increases lipid accumulation and PPARγ abundance, reduces intracellular nicotinamide ade
papers.summary: A genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen in human SW872 preadipocytes identified hundreds of genes regulating white adipocyte differentiation, with integration of human genetic data prioritizing NAPRT. Loss of NAPRT increases lipid accumulation and PPARγ levels while reducing intracellular NAD, suggesting NAPRT normally restrains adipogenesis. This nominates a new metabolic regulator of human fat cell formation.

papers.title: Integrated Experimental and Computational Discovery of the Oxazole-Thiadiazole-Sulfonamide Hybrids as Dual α-Amylase and α-Glucosidase Inhibitors.
papers.abstract: Background: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a major global health concern. Inhibition of α-amylase and α-glucosidase is an established approach to controlling postprandial glucose levels. In this study, we aimed to synthesize oxazole-thiadiazole-sulphonamide derivatives (1-14) and evaluate their inhibitory activity against both enzymes. Methods: Fourteen derivatives were synthesized and characterized using 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and high-resolution electron ionization mass spectrometry (HR-EI-MS). Their inhibitory activities were evaluated using acarbose as the reference inhibitor. Structure-activity rela
papers.summary: The authors synthesized fourteen oxazole-thiadiazole-sulfonamide hybrid compounds and tested them as inhibitors of the diabetes-related enzymes α-amylase and α-glucosidase, using acarbose as a reference drug. Structure-activity relationships were analyzed to identify which chemical features drive potency against both targets. The work is a medicinal chemistry screening study identifying dual inhibitors as potential leads for postprandial glucose control.

papers.title: ATC Classification and Scaffold-Split pMIC Prediction for Antibacterial Prioritization.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance requires reproducible computational tools that distinguish antibacterial-drug class membership from measured antibacterial potency. We developed a descriptor-based workflow for Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification (ATC)-based prioritization, exploratory molecular generation, and pMIC prediction.
papers.summary: The authors present a descriptor-based computational workflow that separates the task of classifying compounds into ATC antibacterial drug classes from predicting measured antibacterial potency (pMIC). The pipeline also includes exploratory molecular generation and a scaffold-split evaluation to support prioritization of candidate antibacterials. It is offered as a reproducible tool for antimicrobial resistance research.

papers.title: Hybrid BiLSTM-Graph Neural Networks Learn Efficient Secondary Structure Representations for Protein-Protein Interface Prediction.
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interfaces (PPIs) are essential for numerous biological processes and represent attractive targets for drug discovery and protein engineering. Although recent protein language models have enabled powerful sequence representations for downstream structural prediction tasks, they require substantial computational resources and produce general-purpose embeddings that are not optimized for specific applications. In this work, we investigate whether task-specific representation learning can provide a computationally efficient alternative for PPI prediction. Proteins are represented
papers.summary: The authors propose a hybrid BiLSTM-graph neural network that learns task-specific protein representations for predicting protein-protein interfaces, arguing this is more computationally efficient than large protein language models. The approach aims to capture secondary structure information directly rather than relying on general-purpose embeddings. The abstract is truncated, so the reported performance and full validation are unclear.

papers.title: Screening and Evaluation of Computationally Predicted JAK1-Binding Candidates from Multi-Source Chemical Space Using Deep Learning and Generative Models.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) is a key mediator in inflammatory and autoimmune signaling pathways and represents a validated therapeutic target. Despite the availability of several JAK inhibitors, challenges in safety and efficacy persist, necessitating further computational prioritization of candidate molecules. Methods: We developed an integrated virtual screening workflow combining ensemble deep learning scoring (KPGT, KarmaDock, DrugCLIP), ADMET-AI filtering, and AutoDock Vina (v1.2.3) docking. The workflow was applied to the NPBS Atlas natural-product database and to molecu
papers.summary: This study builds an integrated virtual screening pipeline that combines ensemble deep-learning scoring (KPGT, KarmaDock, DrugCLIP), ADMET-AI filtering, and AutoDock Vina docking to prioritize JAK1-binding candidates from natural-product and generated chemical libraries. The work demonstrates a practical multi-tool computational workflow for hit triage against a validated inflammatory/autoimmune target, though experimental validation of the top candidates is not reported in the abstract.

papers.title: Accelerating MAPK1 Inhibitor Discovery Through Stacking Ensemble Learning with Graph Neural Networks.
papers.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein kinase 1 (MAPK1) plays a central role in cancer cell proliferation and survival. In this study, we developed an ensemble graph neural network framework integrating graph convolutional neural networks, graph message-passing neural networks, and attention-based graph neural networks to predict MAPK1 inhibitory activity using large-scale quantitative high-throughput screening data. Our models achieved recall ranging from 79.5% to 92.3%, areas under the precision-recall curve ranging from 80.4% to 90.3%, and Matthews correlation coefficients ranging from 0.523 to 0.725 on
papers.summary: The authors built a stacking ensemble of three graph neural network architectures (GCN, MPNN, and attention-based GNN) to predict whether compounds inhibit MAPK1, a kinase central to cancer cell proliferation. Trained on large-scale quantitative high-throughput screening data, the ensemble achieved recall of 79.5–92.3% and precision-recall AUCs of 80.4–90.3%, outperforming individual models. The work offers a computational screening tool to prioritize MAPK1 inhibitor candidates before experimental testing.

papers.title: Learning inhibitor interactions from protein deep mutational scanning data and deep learning models.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in protein language models, geometric deep learning, and structure prediction frameworks have the potential to accelerate computational drug discovery. However, it remains unclear how well these methods generalize beyond their training sets. Mutation-dependent drug responses present a challenge to these methods because there are often large effects from relatively small perturbations. Here, we systematically benchmark diverse mutational effect and drug-target affinity prediction models using deep mutational scanning datasets spanning 11 inhibitor conditions for the MET kinase d
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.summary: This preprint benchmarks protein language models, geometric deep learning, and structure prediction methods on their ability to predict mutation-dependent drug responses, using deep mutational scanning data for the MET kinase across 11 inhibitor conditions. The authors find that these models struggle to generalize beyond their training sets when small mutations cause large changes in inhibitor sensitivity, highlighting a key limitation for computational drug discovery. The work provides a systematic evaluation of how well current deep learning approaches capture mutation-drug interaction effects.

papers.title: Theoretical and Chromatographic Studies to Determine Selected Physicochemical Parameters of 8-Trifluoromethylquinobenzothiazines as Potential Bioactive Compounds.
papers.abstract: Chemical modification of the phenothiazine structure enables the synthesis of promising molecules that are potential candidates for new drugs with a broad spectrum of biological activity. Both computational and experimental methods play a crucial role in the preliminary study of new bioactive compounds, serving to determine various physicochemical properties that influence a compound's ADMET profile, including its lipophilicity.
papers.summary: This study combines computational chemistry and chromatographic experiments to determine physicochemical parameters, especially lipophilicity, of newly synthesized 8-trifluoromethylquinobenzothiazines derived from phenothiazine. These parameters help predict ADMET profiles and assess the compounds' potential as drug candidates. The work supports early-stage prioritization of these bioactive molecules.

papers.title: NFKBIA as a Potential Aging-Related Comorbidity Gene Linking Renal Fibrosis and Age-Associated Muscle Dysfunction: A Hypothesis-Generating Multi-Omics Analysis with Tissue-Specific Regulatory Patterns.
papers.abstract: Aging accelerates renal fibrosis (RF) and age-associated muscle dysfunction (muscle aging), but their shared mechanisms remain unclear. We integrated multi-omics bioinformatics to identify aging-related comorbidity genes linking RF and muscle aging. Bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) used estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and appendicular lean mass (ALM) as proxies for kidney function and muscle mass, followed by differential expression analysis, four machine learning algorithms (LASSO, SVM-RFE, Random Forest, XGBoost), single-cell transcriptomics, pseudotime order
papers.summary: This hypothesis-generating study integrates Mendelian randomization, differential expression, machine learning, and single-cell transcriptomics to identify NFKBIA as a candidate aging-related gene shared between renal fibrosis and age-associated muscle dysfunction. The authors report tissue-specific regulatory patterns for this gene, suggesting a possible common inflammatory mechanism linking kidney and muscle aging. The findings are preliminary and require experimental validation.

papers.title: Computational Identification and Prioritization of Novel Tankyrase 1 and 2 Inhibitor Candidates Through Structure-Based Design, ADMET Profiling, and Long-Timescale Molecular Dynamics.
papers.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains one of the most aggressive breast cancer subtypes and is frequently associated with aberrant activation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Because tankyrase 1 and 2 (TNKS1/2) promote Wnt pathway activation through the regulation of AXIN stability, these enzymes represent attractive therapeutic targets for the development of novel anticancer agents. In this study, an integrated structure-based computational workflow was employed to identify new TNKS1/2 inhibitors. A library comprising known tankyrase inhibitors, structurally related analogues, a
papers.summary: This study uses a computational pipeline combining structure-based drug design, ADMET profiling, and long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations to identify and prioritize novel inhibitor candidates targeting tankyrase 1 and 2 (TNKS1/2) for triple-negative breast cancer. The work leverages the role of TNKS1/2 in stabilizing AXIN and activating the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, proposing new chemical scaffolds as potential anticancer agents. The findings are computational predictions that would require experimental validation.

papers.title: Repurposing of Conivaptan as a Novel Quorum Sensing Inhibitor Against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
papers.abstract: Background: The emergence of multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) poses a significant clinical challenge, necessitating innovative anti-infective strategies. Through high-throughput virtual screening of the DrugBank database, this study identified Conivaptan (hydrochloride, C32H27ClN4O2), an FDA-approved anti-hyponatremia drug, as a potential quorum-sensing inhibitor targeting key regulatory proteins (LasR, RhlR, and PqsR) of P. aeruginosa. Methods: Molecular docking was performed to assess binding interactions with QS regulators. Transcriptomic analysis (RNA-seq) and qua
papers.summary: Using high-throughput virtual screening of DrugBank, the authors identified Conivaptan, an FDA-approved drug for hyponatremia, as a potential quorum-sensing inhibitor targeting the LasR, RhlR, and PqsR regulators of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Molecular docking and transcriptomic (RNA-seq) analyses were used to assess binding and downstream effects, suggesting a possible repurposing strategy against multidrug-resistant infections.

papers.title: From Generative Biology to Evidence-Centric Drug Discovery.
papers.abstract: Generative and predictive artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing the number of molecular, structural, cellular, and therapeutic hypotheses that can be explored computationally. Experimental capacity, however, has not expanded at a comparable rate. The result is an evidence bottleneck, in which biological hypotheses are generated faster than they can be experimentally tested, reproduced, and translated. This mismatch is particularly consequential for pharmaceutical discovery, where computational predictions alone cannot establish biological function, mechanism, or therapeutic value.
papers.summary: This perspective argues that generative and predictive AI now produces biological and therapeutic hypotheses far faster than experiments can validate them, creating an 'evidence bottleneck' in drug discovery. The authors contend that computational predictions alone cannot establish biological function, mechanism, or therapeutic value, and call for a shift toward evidence-centric approaches that prioritize experimental validation and reproducibility.

papers.title: Thiazolyl-Methylthio-1,3,4-Thiadiazolyl-Quinazolin-4(3H)-ones Hybrids: Synthesis, In Silico Profiling, Cytotoxicity, Cellular Death Evaluation, and Effects on Irradiation-Associated DNA Damage.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Combining heterocyclic fragments provides a strategy for developing compounds for exploratory anticancer evaluation. This study aimed to synthesize and characterize five thiazolyl-methylthio-1,3,4-thiadiazolyl-quinazolin-4(3H)-one compounds (5a-e), assess their properties in silico, and investigate the selected ones for cytotoxicity and their effects on irradiation-associated DNA lesions. Methods: Structures were characterized by IR, HRMS, and 1H- and 13C-NMR spectroscopy. Computational studies included physicochemical and ADMETox predictions, multi-platform target predi
papers.summary: This study synthesized five hybrid compounds combining thiazole, thiadiazole, and quinazolinone rings, then characterized them spectroscopically and profiled them computationally for drug-likeness, ADMETox, and predicted targets. Selected compounds were tested for cytotoxicity and for effects on DNA damage associated with irradiation. The work is an exploratory anticancer drug-discovery effort centered on in silico screening plus preliminary cellular assays.

papers.title: RepurposeAD: Knowledge Graph-Guided LLM Reasoning for Alzheimer's Drug Repurposing.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer's disease (AD) drug development continues to suffer from high late-stage attrition and narrow mechanistic diversity, which makes the systematic repurposing of approved compounds an urgent priority. Existing computational repurposing methods operate on fragmented biomedical knowledge, rarely integrate transcriptomic and pharmacological evidence within a single reasoning process, and provide little of the mechanistic transparency required for clinical translation. This paper presents RepurposeAD, a knowledge graph-guided large language model (LLM) reasoning frame
papers.summary: RepurposeAD is a knowledge graph-guided LLM reasoning framework for Alzheimer's drug repurposing that integrates transcriptomic and pharmacological evidence within a single reasoning process. The approach aims to address fragmented biomedical knowledge and lack of mechanistic transparency in existing computational repurposing methods, supporting more clinically translatable candidate prioritization.

papers.title: Characterization and Evaluation of the Neuroprotective Potential of Peptides Derived from Holothuria scabra Inner Wall Proteins: An In Vitro Study.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction driven by interconnected mechanisms, including oxidative stress, apoptosis, and impaired protein homeostasis. Marine-derived proteins and peptides represent promising sources of multifunctional neuroprotective agents; however, the neuroprotective potential of gastrointestinal digestion-derived peptides from Holothuria scabra remains poorly characterized. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of a gastrointestinal digest of H. scabra inner-wall proteins (IWD), a mixture of digestion-derived peptides,
papers.summary: This study characterizes peptides generated by simulated gastrointestinal digestion of inner-wall proteins from the sea cucumber Holothuria scabra and tests their neuroprotective activity in vitro. The digest mixture showed protective effects against mechanisms relevant to neurodegeneration, including oxidative stress, apoptosis, and impaired protein homeostasis. The work positions marine-derived peptides as candidate multifunctional neuroprotective agents, though findings are limited to cell-based assays.

papers.title: From Computational Prioritization to Material Supply: A Proposed Two-Axis Record for Marine Invertebrate-Associated Natural Products and Derivatives.
papers.abstract: Marine natural products can show biological activity while remaining difficult to identify, reproduce, or obtain in sufficient quantity. This critical narrative review examines that mismatch and proposes a linked record for each exact chemical entity-indication pair. The documented evaluation stage (E1-E4) records computational, in vitro, animal, or human evaluation; the production/access stage (S1-S5) records physical access, an executed laboratory route, controlled pilot production, good manufacturing practice (GMP) clinical manufacture, or established commercial manufacture. Neither coordin
papers.summary: This review proposes a two-axis framework for tracking marine invertebrate-derived natural products: an evaluation axis (E1–E4, from computational prediction to human data) and a supply/access axis (S1–S5, from physical availability to commercial manufacture). The goal is to make explicit the frequent mismatch between compounds that look promising computationally or in vitro and those that can actually be produced in sufficient quantity, helping prioritize realistic drug-development candidates.

papers.title: Morus Prenylflavonoids as Candidate NLRP3 Inflammasome Inhibitors from an AI-Guided Natural-Product Screen with a Quantified Applicability Domain.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: The NLRP3 (NACHT, LRR and PYD domains-containing protein 3) inflammasome drives interleukin-1β maturation and pyroptosis in chronic inflammatory disease, and no direct inhibitor has been approved. Natural products are a plausible source of new chemical matter for this target, but such collections are too large to dock exhaustively, and the machine-learning rankings used to triage them are routinely acted on without stating the chemistry over which they hold. This study prioritises natural-product candidates for NLRP3 while quantifying that limit explicitly. Methods: In t
papers.summary: The authors used machine-learning-guided screening to prioritize natural-product candidates as NLRP3 inflammasome inhibitors, focusing on Morus prenylflavonoids. A key methodological contribution is that they explicitly quantified the applicability domain of their ML model, stating the chemical space over which predictions are reliable rather than acting on rankings blindly. This offers a more transparent triage approach for large natural-product libraries targeting an undrugged inflammatory target.

papers.title: Multi-Cohort Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Analyses Identify Six Directionally Concordant Blood-Transcriptomic Signals Associated with Low Bone Mineral Density and Alzheimer's Disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and low bone mineral density (BMD) frequently coexist, but whether they show reproducible concordant blood-transcriptomic signals remains unclear. We conducted a retrospective computational study to identify cross-phenotype expression patterns and explore their biological context.
papers.summary: This retrospective computational study integrated multiple blood transcriptomic cohorts and single-cell data to search for gene-expression signals shared between low bone mineral density and Alzheimer's disease. The authors report six signals whose direction of change is concordant across both phenotypes, suggesting a possible shared blood-based molecular signature. The work is exploratory and does not establish causality or clinical utility.

papers.title: Single-Cell eQTL Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization Analysis Reveals Immune Cell-Specific Genetic Insights into Functional Dyspepsia.
papers.abstract: Background Functional dyspepsia (FD) is a common gastrointestinal disorder characterized by multiple clinical symptoms, complex pathophysiology, and limited therapeutic agents. Emerging evidence indicates a role for immune dysregulation in the pathogenesis of FD; however, immune cell-specific gene regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the genetic factors specific to different immune cell types in FD to explore promising therapeutic targets. Methods We performed Mendelian randomization (MR) and Bayesian colocalization analyses integrating single-cell expression quantitat
papers.summary: This study integrates single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data with Mendelian randomization and Bayesian colocalization to identify immune cell-type-specific genetic factors contributing to functional dyspepsia. The authors link genetic variants to gene expression in specific immune cell populations and assess whether these associations are consistent with causal effects on FD, nominating potential therapeutic targets. The work highlights immune dysregulation as a genetically supported mechanism in FD and demonstrates a framework for cell-type-resolved causal inference.

papers.title: Biophysical and Computational Evidence for Ibuprofen Binding to and Inhibition of MARK4.
papers.abstract: MARK4 is a serine/threonine kinase implicated in neurodegenerative disorders and cancer, making it an attractive target for therapeutic intervention and drug repurposing. In this study, we investigated the inhibition and interaction of ibuprofen with MARK4 using an integrated experimental and computational approach employing steady-state fluorescence and UV-vis spectroscopy, circular dichroism, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. The ATPase assays showed that ibuprofen produces dose-dependent inhibition of MARK4 ATPase activity. The ATPase activity of MARK4 was inhibited by
papers.summary: This study combines experimental biophysical methods (fluorescence, UV-vis, circular dichroism) with computational docking and molecular dynamics to show that ibuprofen binds to and inhibits the kinase MARK4 in a dose-dependent manner. MARK4 is implicated in neurodegenerative disease and cancer, so the finding suggests a potential drug-repurposing opportunity for this common NSAID.

papers.title: ADMET-Stack: quantitative guidance on how much representational complexity an ADMET endpoint actually requires.
papers.abstract: Accurate absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) prediction determines whether a drug candidate survives early development, yet how well it can be predicted depends heavily on how molecules are represented. Previous studies have generally focused on new model architectures, with less attention to the effects of molecular representations and features on ADMET prediction. Here, we evaluated 54 combinations of structural fingerprints, physicochemical descriptors, and SELFIES-derived encodings across all 22 ADMET endpoints of the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) Leader
papers.summary: The authors systematically benchmarked 54 combinations of molecular representations—structural fingerprints, physicochemical descriptors, and SELFIES-derived encodings—across all 22 ADMET endpoints in the Therapeutics Data Commons. They find that the optimal representational complexity varies by endpoint, providing quantitative guidance on how much feature sophistication each ADMET task actually warrants. This shifts attention from model architecture to representation choice as a key driver of ADMET prediction performance.

papers.title: Survival of the fittest tool: choosing between open and closed artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical science.
papers.abstract: Three years ago, this journal published the editorial Technological Darwinism, urging pharmaceutical scientists to adapt to artificial intelligence (AI) rather than resist it. Since then, the question has shifted from whether to use AI to which AI to use, under what circumstances, and with what evidence. This review addresses that question by mapping current AI tools across the five canonical stages of drug development, from discovery to post-market pharmacovigilance. It is a narrative review, not a systematic one, and it treats openness as a spectrum rather than a binary. It compares two broa
papers.journal: Journal of pharmacy & pharmaceutical sciences : a publication of the Canadian Society for Pharmaceutical Sciences, Societe canadienne des sciences pharmaceutiques
papers.summary: This narrative review maps current AI tools across the five canonical stages of drug development, from discovery through post-market pharmacovigilance, and compares open versus closed AI approaches. It argues that openness should be treated as a spectrum rather than a binary and offers guidance on which AI to use, under what circumstances, and with what evidence.

papers.title: Identification and characterization of ion channel-related signatures in ulcerative colitis: an integrated multi-omics and machine learning analysis.
papers.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic, multifactorial inflammatory bowel disease characterized by persistent mucosal inflammation and immune dysregulation. Human ion channel genes (HICGs) are involved in maintaining cellular homeostasis and regulating immune function, but their expression patterns and diagnostic value in UC have not been systematically investigated. This study aimed to identify UC-associated HICGs and evaluate their potential as diagnostic biomarkers using an integrative multi-omics approach.
papers.summary: This study integrates multi-omics data with machine learning to identify ion channel genes whose expression patterns distinguish ulcerative colitis from healthy tissue. The authors propose these genes as candidate diagnostic biomarkers, though the abstract does not report specific validated findings. The work is exploratory and biomarker-oriented rather than mechanistic.

papers.title: GPCRVS in the detection of target-selective molecular scaffolds based on deep learning and gradient boosting.
papers.abstract: High drug selectivity minimizes unintended interactions that cause adverse effects, decreases drug potency, and are failure-prone factors in many clinical trials due to a poor balance between drug efficacy and toxicity. Sharing similar structural folds and modes of activation, G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR) may represent difficult drug targets in terms of optimization of pharmacodynamic profiles towards drug target selectivity. Here, we describe GPCRVS, a web service for GPCR virtual screening, designed to detect selective drug-like compounds. GPCRVS combines machine learning for ligand-ba
papers.summary: GPCRVS is a new web service that combines deep learning and gradient boosting to virtually screen chemical compounds for selectivity toward specific G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a protein family where achieving drug target selectivity is notoriously difficult. The tool aims to help identify drug-like molecules that preferentially bind one GPCR over closely related ones, potentially reducing side effects and improving clinical trial success rates.

papers.title: From AI-Generated Sequences to Therapeutic Peptide Candidates: A Disease-First Perspective on Computational Design, Developability, and Application.
papers.abstract: Therapeutic peptides bridge the gap between small-molecule drugs and biologics, offering high target selectivity and broad opportunities for chemical and structural optimization. However, their clinical translation remains constrained by proteolytic instability, limited bioavailability, delivery barriers, safety concerns, and manufacturing challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI) expands the generation and prioritization of peptide hypotheses through language models, target-conditioned design, structure-aware modeling, and multi-objective optimization. Experimental testing of disease-relevant
papers.summary: This review examines how AI methods—including language models, target-conditioned design, structure-aware modeling, and multi-objective optimization—are being used to generate and prioritize therapeutic peptide candidates. It frames the discussion around disease-first design and the practical barriers to clinical translation, such as proteolytic instability, poor bioavailability, delivery issues, safety, and manufacturing challenges.

papers.title: AI-driven transformation of GPCR research: from structural biology to precision medicine.
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) regulate complex pathophysiological networks and represent a critical class of drug targets, but their structural determination and ligand screening are constrained by dependence on homology templates, static conformations, and a bias toward known ligands. Artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming GPCR structural biology and pharmacology by overcoming these bottlenecks. The methodologies encompass high-precision static structure prediction, dynamic conformational ensemble modeling, ultra-large-scale virtual screening, de novo ligand design, allos
papers.summary: This review describes how artificial intelligence is transforming G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) research, moving beyond traditional homology-based structural biology and static models. AI methods now enable high-precision structure prediction, dynamic conformational ensemble modeling, ultra-large-scale virtual screening, and de novo ligand design, with the goal of advancing precision medicine for this major drug target class.

papers.title: Identification of potential natural PPARγ agonists via graph neural networks and integrated computational approaches.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus has become a prevalent metabolic disease worldwide. Current synthetic PPARγ (Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ)agonists are associated with adverse effects, highlighting the need to explore natural compounds with potential PPARγ agonistic activity. PPARγ is a vital therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes. To facilitate the discovery of natural PPARγ agonists, this study integrated graph neural network (GNN) prediction, molecular docking, ADMET evaluation, in vitro activity assessment, and molecular dynamics simulations for multistage virtual screening. Three
papers.summary: This study combines graph neural network prediction, molecular docking, ADMET evaluation, in vitro assays, and molecular dynamics simulations to screen natural compounds for PPARγ agonist activity, a target for type 2 diabetes. The multistage virtual screening pipeline identified three candidate natural compounds with potential PPARγ agonistic activity, offering a computational strategy to prioritize natural product drug discovery.

papers.title: A Machine-Learning Framework Integrating Frequency-Domain Spectral Features for Ligand Classification and Candidate Prioritization.
papers.abstract: AI-assisted drug discovery (AIDD) combines molecular modeling with machine learning to support lead identification and candidate prioritization. Conventional molecular descriptors principally encode static chemical structures, leaving frequency-domain behavior as an additional source of molecular information. We therefore developed the terahertz fusion descriptor (THz-FD), a feature-fusion framework that integrates terahertz (THz) frequency-domain features for Na+/K+-ATPase ligand classification and retrospective ranking. Extra Trees (ET), Random Forest (RF), and support vector machine (SVM) c
papers.summary: The authors introduce THz-FD, a feature-fusion framework that combines conventional molecular descriptors with terahertz frequency-domain spectral features to classify Na+/K+-ATPase ligands and prioritize candidates. Using Extra Trees, Random Forest, and SVM classifiers, they show that adding frequency-domain information can improve ligand classification and retrospective ranking. The work suggests spectral behavior as a complementary signal for AI-assisted drug discovery.

papers.title: Identification of dihydrokaempferol from Platycladus orientalis leaves as a potential therapeutic candidate for androgenetic alopecia through modulation of the KIT-mediated mast cell axis.
papers.abstract: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA) is the most common form of hair loss, characterized by progressive follicular miniaturization. Current therapies mainly target androgen signaling and show limited efficacy. Emerging evidence indicates that immune dysregulation contributes to AGA progression, but its therapeutic implications remain unclear. This study aimed to identify active compounds from Platycladus orientalis leaves and investigate their mechanisms in regulating AGA.
papers.summary: This study identifies dihydrokaempferol, a compound from Platycladus orientalis leaves, as a potential treatment for androgenetic alopecia (common hair loss). The authors show it may work by modulating the KIT-mediated mast cell axis, suggesting immune regulation—rather than just androgen signaling—as a therapeutic target. This points to a plant-derived candidate for a condition with limited treatment options.

papers.title: An integrated computational and experimental framework identifies apigenin as a potential therapeutic agent targeting EGFR/STAT3/MMP9 signaling in glioma.
papers.abstract: Glioma is the most common primary malignant tumor of the central nervous system and is characterized by aggressive progression, high recurrence rates, and limited therapeutic options. Apigenin, a naturally occurring flavonoid, exhibits promising anti-tumor properties; however, its molecular mechanisms in glioma remain insufficiently understood. To systematically identify the therapeutic targets and molecular mechanisms underlying apigenin-mediated anti-glioma activity through an integrated computational and experimental approach.
papers.summary: This study combines computational target prediction with experimental validation to identify apigenin, a natural flavonoid, as a potential anti-glioma agent acting through the EGFR/STAT3/MMP9 signaling axis. The integrated framework links network pharmacology predictions to in vitro evidence, suggesting apigenin may suppress glioma progression by disrupting this signaling pathway.

papers.title: Subtractive Genomic Approach for Identification of Pathogen-Specific Essential Genes as Target and Drug Repurposing in Major Foodborne Bacteria.
papers.abstract: Foodborne diseases pose a substantial threat to global public health and economic stability, with bacterial contamination occurring at multiple stages of the food supply chain. The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among foodborne pathogens has further complicated the prevention and treatment of these infections, underscoring the urgent need for novel, pathogen-specific therapeutic targets. In this study, a comprehensive subtractive genomics approach was employed to systematically identify bacterial key genes (bKGs) as drug targets and to explore corresponding potential therape
papers.summary: This study applies a subtractive genomics pipeline to identify essential genes in major foodborne bacterial pathogens that are absent from the human host, yielding candidate pathogen-specific drug targets. The authors then pair these targets with drug repurposing screens to propose existing compounds as potential antimicrobials. The work is a computational target-discovery exercise aimed at addressing antimicrobial resistance in foodborne pathogens.
